projects.title: AI Job Application Tracker
projects.label: Product Workflow
projects.description: A React tracker for job applications — statuses, filters, notes, and a mock REST API, with loading and empty states.
projects.summary: A React tracker for job applications — statuses, filters, notes, and a mock REST API, with loading and empty states.

caseStudy.intro: I built this to practice a product workflow, not a static table. Applications move through statuses, filters stay in sync, and the list talks to a small mock API. I used AI to sketch the data shape and empty states, then wrote and reviewed the React myself.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.body: A spreadsheet of applications is hard to scan. I needed a UI a junior applicant would actually use: status, company, role, and notes, with filters that do not reset, and an empty state that is honest when the list is new.

sections.title: The approach
sections.body: TypeScript types the application record. Fetch wrappers cover loading, error, and retry. Filters are React state over the same list used by the table. I used Cursor to draft the filter logic, then simplified it in review so I could explain every branch.

sections.title: The outcome
sections.body: The demo is on Vercel and the repo is on GitHub. It is the project I use to talk about REST-shaped data, forms, and AI as a helper — not as the author of the final code.

highlights: Status filters over a mock REST API
Notes and validation on each application

projects.title: Fintech Analytics Dashboard
projects.label: React Dashboard
projects.description: A React dashboard for payments-style data — charts, filters, and a table, with API-shaped JSON and keyboard-friendly rows.
projects.summary: A React dashboard for payments-style data — charts, filters, and a table, with API-shaped JSON and keyboard-friendly rows.

caseStudy.intro: I built this as a Next.js practice project for dense product UI: a persistent filter bar, a main chart, and a table underneath. Metrics come from JSON shaped like a REST payload so the pattern would transfer to a real endpoint.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.body: Tutorial dashboards skip filters and error states. I wanted a layout that still works when the request is slow, empty, or fails, and a table a keyboard user can scan.

sections.title: The approach
sections.body: React state owns the filters. Recharts draws the main chart. TypeScript keeps the metric shape honest. I used AI to refactor repetitive table cells, then reviewed the diff before committing.

sections.title: The outcome
sections.body: On GitHub and Vercel. Adding a metric is a data change, not a layout rewrite — the same habit I would use on an internal tools team.

highlights: Loading and empty states for the table

projects.title: Store Operations Dashboard
projects.label: Internal Dashboard
projects.description: A React dashboard for a store owner — revenue, orders, inventory, and traffic — fed by JSON shaped like a REST payload.
projects.summary: A React dashboard for a store owner — revenue, orders, inventory, and traffic — with charts, tables, and API-shaped JSON.

caseStudy.intro: Practice for an internal merchant tool: one home screen with metrics, a sales chart, recent orders, and stock status. Numbers come from JSON shaped like a dashboard endpoint so the layout would transfer to a real API.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.body: A store owner needs the day’s numbers in one place — revenue, orders, and what is out of stock — without hopping between reports. Tutorial dashboards often skip empty rows and treat every widget as a static mock.

sections.title: The approach
sections.body: TypeScript types the metric, order, and inventory records. The chart and the orders table read the same JSON. Status chips on orders and stock stay labels, not decoration. Loading and empty states are real screens if the payload is slow or missing.

sections.title: The outcome
sections.body: A small internal-dashboard demo on Vercel. I use it to talk about dense product UI, tables, and API-shaped records — not about running a shop.

highlights: Revenue and order metrics from JSON
Inventory status on the same home screen

projects.title: E-commerce Product Explorer
projects.label: React Storefront
projects.description: A product explorer with catalog filters, variants, a cart drawer, and catalog data from JSON shaped like a catalog API.
projects.summary: A product-first React storefront — catalog, variants, cart drawer, and an accessible checkout UI.

caseStudy.intro: Practice for catalog UI: a filterable grid, a detail page with variants, and a cart drawer. Products come from JSON shaped like a catalog endpoint.

sections.title: The challenge
sections.body: Theme-style demos hide variants in too many dropdowns. I wanted a storefront a keyboard user could finish, with an empty cart state that is not a dead end.

sections.title: The approach
sections.body: Grid first, then a detail page with one variant control. The cart is a drawer. Labels and focus states are written for a keyboard. Filters run over the same product list the grid uses.

sections.title: The outcome
sections.body: Swapping products is a JSON change. Demo on Vercel, repo on GitHub — a walkthrough of lists, filters, and cart state, not a claim that I shipped a real store.
